question: How do the leading open-weight coding models compare on coding skill and on speed/throughput on 128 GB-class unified memory hardware (NVIDIA DGX Spark GB10 class), from named benchmark harnesses?

crown.swebench_verified_default_board: Best open-weight-family row as fetched: MiniMax M2.5 (high) 75.80 via mini-SWE-agent (bash-only Verified, 2026-02-17); runner-up open-family row GLM 5 (high) 72.80 — margin 3.00 points. Caveat: swebench.com does not label licenses; openness of the GLM/Kimi/DeepSeek/gpt-oss families is grounded on the Fireworks/Artificial Analysis pages, MiniMax M2.5's license is not stated on any fetched page.
crown.aa_coding_index: Verbatim crown from the dated Fireworks table (updated 4.27.26): 'The top open-source spot on the AA Coding Index is now a near-tie between DeepSeek V4-Pro (47.5) and Kimi K2.6 (47.1)' — margin 0.4 points, composite of Terminal-Bench Hard and SciCode.
crown.on_the_128gb_machine: The local-speed crown and the coding-skill crown go to different models: gpt-oss-120b is the biggest model that decodes fluently on a single Spark (58.82 tok/s vLLM single node per Spark Arena quote; ~50 tok/s community per sayob) but scores 26.00 on SWE-bench Verified via mini-SWE-agent and 28.6 on the AA Coding Index; the SWE-bench open leaders (MiniMax M2.5 75.80, GLM 5 72.80, Kimi K2.5 70.80) are full-size models whose local 128 GB quantized throughput was not measured on any fetched page.

FINDINGS.claim: Official SWE-bench Verified leaderboard now defaults to a bash-only setting run with mini-SWE-agent, on a human-filtered 500-instance subset — the harness and setting every Verified number below carries.
FINDINGS.verbatim_quote: _Verified_ is a human-filtered subset of 500 instances ( [details](https://openai.com/index/introducing-swe-bench-verified/)). Defaults to [_bash-only_](https://www.swebench.com/bash-only) setting (run with [mini-SWE-agent](https://github.com/SWE-agent/mini-swe-agent)).

FINDINGS.claim: On the default (bash-only, mini-SWE-agent) SWE-bench Verified board, MiniMax M2.5 (high) posts the highest score among open-weight-family rows fetched: 75.80% at $0.07 per run, dated 2026-02-17 — the best open coding score found this session.
Runner-up open-family rows on the same board: GLM 5 (high) 72.80%, Kimi K2.5 (high) 70.80%, DeepSeek V3.2 (high) 70.00% — so the SWE-bench open crown margin is 3.00 points (75.80 vs 72.80).
GLM-4.6's best Verified row on the official board is 68.20% with an Undisclosed agent (dated 2025-09-30, exactly one year before this brief); under mini-SWE-agent it drops to 55.40% at $0.10.

Other named open coding models on Verified: Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B-Instruct 69.60% with OpenHands (2025-08-05) / 55.40% with mini-SWE-agent; Kimi K2 71.20% with Lingxi v1.5; Kimi K2 Thinking 63.40%; Devstral Small (2512) 56.40%; gpt-oss-120b just 26.00% at $0.06.

The AA Coding Index (composite of Terminal-Bench Hard and SciCode, per a Fireworks table last updated 4.27.26) crowns DeepSeek V4-Pro the best open coder by 0.4 points over Kimi K2.6 — a near-tie, with gpt-oss-120B far behind at 28.6.
FINDINGS.verbatim_quote: The top open-source spot on the AA Coding Index is now a near-tie between DeepSeek V4-Pro (47.5) and Kimi K2.6 (47.1), both live on Fireworks Serverless. V4-Pro edges the composite and leads on Terminal-Bench Hard (0.462 vs 0.439); Kimi K2.6 leads on AA Intelligence (53.9 vs 52) and SciCode (0.535 vs 0.500).

FINDINGS.claim: The GB10's decode ceiling is bandwidth-bound vs Apple silicon: gpt-oss-20b measured 84.67 tokens/sec on Spark vs 117.32 tokens/sec on MacBook Pro M4 Max (same llama-server command), with the follow-up explanation that M4 Max has double the memory bandwidth while Spark wins prompt processing.
FINDINGS.verbatim_quote: The result 84.67 tokens/sec ... The result 117.32 tokens/sec ... Well, yes, M4 Max has double memory bandwidth compared to Spark, so inference will be faster. Prompt processing, however, is faster on Spark because of better GPU.

FINDINGS.claim: A July 2026 DGX Spark roundup attributes 273 GB/s memory bandwidth and gives community-measured decode by model: gpt-oss-120b ~50 tok/s at ~60-65 GB FP4 (fluent), Qwen3 Coder 30B ~44 tok/s, gpt-oss-20b ~68 tok/s, dense 70B only 2.5-5 tok/s; prefill ~1,900 tok/s class; its coding pick is Qwen3 Coder 30B.
FINDINGS.verbatim_quote: Memory moves at 273 GB/s, and every generated token requires reading all _active_ weights. ... | gpt-oss-120b | MoE, 120B total | ~60–65 GB (FP4) | ~50 tok/s | Flagship-quality chat, genuinely fluent | ... | Qwen3 Coder 30B | MoE | ~18–20 GB | ~44 tok/s | Strong coding assistant speed | ... | Llama-class dense 70B | Dense | ~40 GB (Q4) / ~70 GB (FP8) | ~2.5–5 tok/s | Fits fine; too slow for interactive chat |

MISCONCEPTIONS.myth: 128 GB of unified memory means you can run the best open coding model locally at chat speed.
MISCONCEPTIONS.reality: The harness-crowned best open coders (MiniMax M2.5 at 75.80, GLM 5 at 72.80, Kimi K2.5 at 70.80 on SWE-bench Verified; DeepSeek V4-Pro/Kimi K2.6 on the AA Coding Index) are full-scale models whose quantized 128 GB throughput nobody measured on fetched pages; the model actually crowned fastest big decode on one Spark, gpt-oss-120b at 58.82 tok/s, scores only 26.00 on the same Verified board and 28.6 on the AA Coding Index.

MISCONCEPTIONS.myth: A dense 70B model is the quality play on a 128 GB machine — it fits, so it will be usable.
MISCONCEPTIONS.reality: It fits (~40 GB at Q4) but decodes at ~2.5–5 tok/s because memory moves at 273 GB/s and dense models must read all weights every token — 'Fits fine; too slow for interactive chat.'

MISCONCEPTIONS.myth: More memory means faster inference — the Spark's 128 GB beats a Mac.
MISCONCEPTIONS.reality: Decode is bandwidth-bound, not capacity-bound: gpt-oss-20b ran 84.67 tokens/sec on Spark vs 117.32 tokens/sec on MacBook Pro M4 Max, because 'M4 Max has double memory bandwidth compared to Spark'; Spark wins prompt processing instead.

MISCONCEPTIONS.myth: One coding benchmark tells you which open model is best.
MISCONCEPTIONS.reality: Crowns flip with the harness: gpt-oss-120b is near-bottom on AA's composite (28.6, Terminal-Bench Hard 0.235) yet competitive on LiveCodeBench (0.878); GLM-4.6 spans 68.20 (Undisclosed agent) to 55.40 (mini-SWE-agent) on the same Verified set depending on the agent harness.

MISCONCEPTIONS.myth: Big-MoE decode speed on the Spark is fixed hardware fate.
MISCONCEPTIONS.reality: Software moved the numbers: the maintainer thread logged improvements from b6761 (Oct 2025) through b7946 (Feb 2026), the community built a reproducible leaderboard (Spark Arena, Feb 11, 2026) after 'everyone posts partial flags, then nobody can reproduce it two weeks later', and vLLM's 58.82 tok/s single-node beats llama.cpp's 45.34 t/s tg128 on the same model.

GLOSSARY.definition: Human-filtered 500-instance subset of SWE-bench (real GitHub issues); the official leaderboard currently defaults to a bash-only setting run with mini-SWE-agent. Scores are % resolved and depend on both model and agent harness.
Minimal bash-only agent harness the official SWE-bench Verified leaderboard defaults to; the same model can score much lower under it than under heavier bespoke agents.
Artificial Analysis composite of Terminal-Bench Hard (end-to-end shell agentic tasks) and SciCode (scientific code generation); higher is better.
pp = prompt prefill (tokens ingested per second); tg = text generation/decode. 'tg128 @ d48000' = decode 128 tokens at a 48k-token context depth.

Mixture-of-Experts models load all weights but activate a small slice per token (e.g. gpt-oss-120b: 117B total, 5.1B active) — why a 59 GiB model decodes fluently on 273 GB/s memory while a 40 GB dense 70B cannot.
Weight-quantization formats (4-bit MXFP4 and NVFP4, 8-bit FP8, 4-bit GGUF Q4) that shrink model footprint; every throughput number carries its quant.
Single 128 GB LPDDR5x pool shared by CPU and Blackwell GPU on DGX Spark — no VRAM wall, but ~110–115 GB practical headroom and 273 GB/s bandwidth cap.
Community reproducibility leaderboard for DGX Spark inference (launched Feb 11, 2026) with agreed recipes; cited here secondhand through the llama.cpp discussion.

UNVERIFIED: The Spark Arena values (gpt-oss-120b 58.82 tok/s single node, 75.96 tok/s two nodes, Qwen3-Coder-Next 60.51 tok/s, Nemotron-3-Nano-30B 56.11 tok/s) are a user's quote of spark-arena.com inside the llama.cpp thread; spark-arena.com itself was not fetched, and the benchmark setting for those rows is not stated in the quote.

sayob.com's per-model decode speeds (~50 tok/s gpt-oss-120b, ~44 tok/s Qwen3 Coder 30B, ~2.5–5 tok/s dense 70B, ~1,900 tok/s prefill) are described as 'community-measured decode speeds' with no per-number method, engine, or quant named beyond FP4/Q4 sizes.
